MS-2026-HB1152.s: The bill would set up a way for some people with chronic, worsening, severe, or terminal illnesses to be reviewed for the state medical cannabis program, even if they do not meet the current qualifying condition rule. Their treating medical provider could ask the state health department for approval, and the state health officer would make the final decision. If approved, the patient could apply for a registry card and would be checked again at least once every 12 months.

MS-2026-HB1648.s: This act brings forward several budget laws and rules about how Mississippi makes and balances its budget. It also directs the State Fiscal Officer to make certain transfers to the Capital Expense Fund during fiscal year 2027. The act keeps rules for the Working Cash-Stabilization Reserve Fund and the Capital Expense Fund, and it affects state budget agencies and state funds.

MS-2026-HB1653.s: This bill would change the allowed uses of money for certain local improvement projects and college capital projects funded in 2022, 2023, and 2024. It affects some projects paid for with the Local Improvements Projects Fund and the IHL Capital Improvements Fund in Mississippi.

MS-2026-HB1924.s: Would provide funding to cover the expenses of the Mississippi Attorney General’s office for fiscal year 2027. It affects the office that handles the state’s top legal work.

MS-2026-HB4011.s: The bill would extend the law that creates the Jackson Convention and Visitors Bureau and funds it from taxes on hotel, motel, and restaurant sales. It would also allow an extra 1% tax on hotel and motel sales and a 1/2% tax on restaurant sales. An election would be held on whether the new tax may be levied.

MS-2026-HB4013.s: The bill would extend the repeal date for Moss Point’s restaurant tax from July 1, 2026, to July 1, 2030. It would keep in place the city’s power to charge an added sales tax of up to 2% on prepared food sold by restaurants in the city.

MS-2026-HB4038.s: The bill would let the City of Greenwood set up a registration program for vacant and abandoned buildings. It would affect property in Greenwood that is empty or abandoned.

MS-2026-HB4100.s: The measure would let the DeSoto County Board of Supervisors buy radar speed equipment for the sheriff’s department to help enforce speed limits on county roads and state highways outside city limits. Money from using that equipment would go to resource officers in DeSoto County public schools. It died in committee.

MS-2026-HB4114.s: The bill would extend the repeal date for the Hattiesburg Tourism Commission and the local hotel and motel tax from July 1, 2027, to July 1, 2031. The tax is charged on overnight room rentals and helps fund the commission.

MS-2026-HB4121.s: The bill would restore the right to vote to Wykesia Geater of Jackson County, Mississippi. It affects one named person. The measure passed the House and was sent to the Senate, where it later died in committee.

MS-2026-HB4122.s: The bill would restore the right to vote to Cleveland Stallworth of Jackson County, Mississippi. It affects one named person and would give back his suffrage rights.

MS-2026-HB4124.s: Would restore voting rights to Jerome Wyatt of Jones County, Mississippi.

MS-2026-HB4125.s: The bill would restore the right to vote to Omar Travis of Hinds County, Mississippi. It applies to that one person and would return his voting rights if enacted.

MS-2026-HB4128.s: The bill would restore voting rights to Omar Eugene Magee of Covington County, Mississippi. It affects only that named person.

MS-2026-HB4129.s: The bill would restore the right to vote, also called suffrage, to Christopher Preston of Covington County, Mississippi. It affects only that person. The measure passed the House and was later sent to the Senate, but it died in committee.

MS-2026-HB4131.s: Would restore the right to vote, called suffrage, to Larry Mangum of Hinds County, Mississippi. It affects only him.

MS-2026-HB4141.s: The bill would restore Peter Fulton’s right to vote in Mississippi. It affects Peter Fulton of Oktibbeha County and no money amount is stated.

MS-2026-HB4145.s: The bill would extend the repeal date of a law that lets the City of Richland charge a 3% tax on hotel and motel room rentals. The money would be used to support tourism and parks and recreation in the city. It would affect hotels, motels, and people who rent rooms there.

MS-2026-HB4160.s: Would restore the right to vote, called suffrage, to Herman Howard of Hinds County, Mississippi. It affects only that one person.

MS-2026-HB4162.s: Would restore voting rights to Joe Nelson London of Lee County, Mississippi.

MS-2026-HB4167.s: Would restore the right to vote, called the right of suffrage, to Jon E. Walker of Benton County, Mississippi.

MS-2026-HB4172.s: The bill would let the Jackson County Board of Supervisors create a public improvement district. The district could hold an election to approve a retail assessment, which is a charge on retail sales inside the district. Money from that assessment could be used with other district funds, and the district would have to keep separate records and get an annual audit.

MS-2026-HB4175.s: Would restore voting rights, called the right of suffrage, to Charles Covington of Lee County, Mississippi. It would apply to one named person only.

MS-2026-HB4179.s: The bill would restore voting rights to Jennifer Miles of Winston County, Mississippi.

MS-2026-HB4183.s: The bill would change how the City of Laurel uses some money from a recreation and public improvement promotion tax and certain bonds. It would stop that portion of the money from being used to pay for building and equipping improvements at the fairground complex. It affects the city government and how it spends those funds.

MS-2026-HB895.s: The bill would change Mississippi medical cannabis rules by ending the required six-month follow-up visit after a patient gets certification, while still letting the practitioner ask for one if needed. It would also extend some certification and ID card validity periods to 24 months, or two years. It would remove THC potency limits for cannabis tinctures, oils, and concentrates.

MS-2026-HC5.s: This resolution would ask a congressional committee to approve replacing the statues of James Zachariah George and Jefferson Davis in Statuary Hall with statues of Fannie Lou Hamer and Senator Hiram Rhodes Revels. It affects the display of Mississippi statues in the U.S. Capitol.

MS-2026-HC50.s: A concurrent resolution would condemn the arson attack on Beth Israel Congregation on January 10, 2026. It affects the congregation and records lawmakers’ formal statement of disapproval.

MS-2026-HC51.s: The resolution would have Mississippi ask for a U.S. constitutional convention under Article V to consider term limits for members of Congress. A concurrent resolution is a formal statement by lawmakers. It affects the state’s request for that national process.

MS-2026-HC65.s: A concurrent resolution would suspend deadlines so House Bill 938 could keep moving forward. It would also extend the repeal dates on several Mississippi youth court laws, including rules on youth court records, intake reporting, the youth court support program and fund, limits on access to MYCIDS, and a parent’s power to delegate child care and custody duties.

MS-2026-HR154.s: This resolution would honor Confederate Memorial Day and remember Mississippians who served in the Civil War. It would also encourage people in Mississippi to reflect on the history and lessons of that time.

MS-2026-HR169.s: This resolution says certain property in Jackson should be sold or leased. It says the move would be to create value, protect the local environment, support economic growth, and add to the city's tax base.

MS-2026-JR201.s: The resolution would change a 2025 redistricting measure so that, if the U.S. Supreme Court makes a final ruling in the Louisiana congressional redistricting case that the plan breaks the U.S. Constitution or cannot be decided by the court, the current state Senate district plan would be replaced by a 2022 resolution. It affects Mississippi Senate districts. It died in committee.

MS-2026-SB2210.s: The bill would let Bolivar County set up a utility district in the Choctaw community to own, run, and keep up the Choctaw Sewer Association system. It would also let the county transfer property to the district and provide money and services for sewer repairs and improvements.

MS-2026-SB2632.s: Would create a state loan program run by the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency to help local governments recover from certain federally declared disasters. It would give loans from a new state fund and require the local government to repay the money, using set local revenue if federal reimbursement does not come through. The bill would also let the agency skip some state contract review steps for work tied to the program.

MS-2026-SB2930.s: The bill would extend the date when the law ends for Southaven’s tax on sales of drinks and prepared food at restaurants in the city. It affects restaurants in Southaven that sell those items.

MS-2026-SB3106.s: The bill would extend the law that created the Jackson Convention and Visitors Bureau and the tax used to fund it. It would also let Jackson add a 1% tax on hotel and motel sales and a 1/2% tax on restaurant sales, if voters approve the tax in an election. These changes would affect hotels, motels, restaurants, and the bureau in Jackson.

MS-2026-SB3108.s: The bill would let Pass Christian city police use one radar speed device to check and enforce speed limits on parts of U.S. Highway 90 inside the city limits. It died in committee.

MS-2026-SB3231.s: The bill would let Noxubee County leaders ask voters to approve a 2% tax on room rentals at hotels, motels, and bed and breakfasts in the county. The tax would not apply to rentals of 30 days or more. Money from the tax would go to tourism and to parks and recreation.

MS-2026-SB3383.s: Would let the Lee County Board of Supervisors buy radar speed detection gear for the sheriff’s department to help enforce school zone speed limits on county roads and state highways outside city limits. It applies to Lee County and its sheriff’s department.

MS-2026-SB3387.s: The city of Hattiesburg would be allowed to make a long-term lease for city-owned property for up to 30 years. It would affect the city’s governing officials and any lease of that property.

MS-2026-SB3391.s: Forrest County officials would be allowed to buy radar speed detection equipment for the sheriff’s department. The equipment would be used to help enforce speed limits on county roads and state highways outside city limits.

MS-2026-SB3397.s: This bill would restore the right to vote to Frankie O'Neal Ward, Jr. of Jefferson Davis County, Mississippi. It applies to that one person.

MS-2026-SB3409.s: The bill would let the Lowndes County Board of Supervisors create an industrial zone emergency response district. It would let the district charge special assessments to industrial taxpayers based on property value and the number of employees they keep in the district, to fund the district’s work. It would also let the district issue bonds or other debt and would exempt its property and revenue from state, county, and city taxes.

MS-2026-SC530.s: A concurrent resolution is a formal statement by lawmakers. It would ask Congress to call a convention of the states to propose a U.S. Constitution amendment that sets term limits for members of the U.S. House and Senate.

MS-2026-SC532.s: This resolution would ask the U.S. Supreme Court to overturn the Obergefell v. Hodges decision. It would also call for states to regain the power to set the rules for marriage and divorce.

MS-2026-SC533.s: This concurrent resolution would express the Mississippi Legislature’s sympathy to the family of Reverend Jesse L. Jackson, Sr. after his passing. It is a formal statement of support and condolence.

MS-2026-SC535.s: The resolution would direct the Mississippi Department of Finance and Administration to bar the display of the LGBTQ pride, or rainbow, flag on any state building or local government building. It would affect state agencies and political subdivisions, which are local government bodies.

MS-2026-SC545.s: A concurrent resolution would honor Carroll E. Rhodes for a lifetime of service to civil rights, the rule of law, and the people of Mississippi.

MS-2026-SR27.s: A resolution is a formal statement from lawmakers. It would call on Congress to pass bills that repeal the federal FACE Act and would commend President Trump for pardons he issued to 23 people convicted under that law.

MS-2026-SR58.s: A Mississippi resolution would urge the U.S. Congress to pass the Major Richard Star Act. The act would aim to let veterans with disabilities receive both their full Defense Department retirement pay and their VA disability pay. It would affect veterans with disabilities who get both kinds of payments.

MS-2026-SR6.s: The resolution would ask the U.S. Congress to pass a law that adds airguns and airbows to the items taxed under the federal Wildlife Restoration Program, also called the Pittman-Robertson Act. It would affect those products by placing them in the same tax program as other hunting items covered by that law.

MS-2026-SR78.s: The resolution would condemn the killing of Charles "Charlie" James Kirk and all forms of political violence. It would also honor his legacy.

MS-2026-SR97.s: A resolution would encourage education and outreach to help the public understand the role of regulated trapping in managing wildlife. It applies to public information about how trapping fits into wildlife management.

MS-20261E-HB1.s: Mississippi lawmakers approved a change to how certain state funds for the Department of Human Services can be used for a youth diversion program in fiscal year 2027. The bill affects that department and the money set aside for this program. It was approved by the governor.

MS-20261E-HB2.s: This law gives extra general fund and special fund money for fiscal year 2027 to cover costs at the Department of Human Services and the Department of Public Safety. It affects those two state agencies. It was approved by the governor.

MS-20261E-HR1.s: The resolution honors Representative James Price Wallace for his public service and expresses sympathy after his death. It was adopted and later signed.

MS-20261E-HR2.s: This resolution mourns the death of William R. "Bo" Brown and honors his life, public service, and work as a lawmaker. It also offers sympathy to his family and friends. The measure was adopted and signed.

MS-20261E-SB2001.s: This law changes how youth court cases are handled in Mississippi. It sets new rules for youth court judges and staff, ends some old youth court offices and roles in 2027, and creates a new family services forum for children, youth, and families. It also bars new county youth courts after the law takes effect and requires some counties to decide by December 1, 2028, whether to keep their own youth court divisions at their own expense. The bill was signed by the governor on July 17, 2026.

MS-20261E-SB2002.s: The bill would extend the repeal dates for several sections of Mississippi law, including rules tied to youth court and one sex offender registration section. It affects those laws by keeping them in place longer before they would expire.

MS-20261E-SB2003.s: The bill would provide extra state money for fiscal year 2027 to help pay expenses for the Department of Human Services and the Department of Public Safety. It is tied to youth court reform in Mississippi.

MS-20261E-SB2004.s: The bill would revise how some fiscal year 2027 money for the Department of Human Services is used for a youth diversion program. It would change the purpose of those funds. It was referred to appropriations and later died on the calendar.
